Customer has compliance questions (SOC2, audit logs) and VPC constraints; agreed next steps to share security docs and run a PoC benchmark next week.
topics: SDK quickstart; auth (API keys vs SSO); environment variables and secrets (KMS/HSM note); python example; typescript example; streaming & callbacks; batching & cost controls; deployment modes (hosted vs dedicated vs private); PoC plan and success metrics; security/Q&A
transcript:
[00:00] Evan Martinez: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:05] Liam O'Connor: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:07] Evan Martinez: Great. Quick intros — Evan with Redwood, AE, and Priya Desai our solutions engineer.
[00:12] Priya Desai: Hi all.
[00:13] Sara Chen: Sara here, backend.
[00:15] Marcus Lee: Marcus, DevOps.
[00:17] Ana Torres: Ana from product.
[00:19] Evan Martinez: Awesome. Today we'll run through the SDK integration quickstarts in Python and TypeScript, auth patterns, environment setup, and show a small demo of streaming responses. Then we'll leave time for security and PoC questions.
[00:35] Evan Martinez: Priya do you want to kick us off with the Python quickstart?
[00:40] Priya Desai: Sure. I'm going to share my screen — let me know if you can see the repo.
[00:45] Marcus Lee: Seeing it. There is some lag but it's fine.
[00:47] Priya Desai: Cool. In the README we have a minimal pip install, then export REDWOOD_API_KEY as the env var. Example code is four lines: import redwood, client = redwood.Client(), response = client.generate("prompt") — we try to keep the surface tiny.
[01:10] Sara Chen: Is the package name pip install redwood-inference?
[01:12] Priya Desai: It's redwood-inference for now, yes. We also show how to pin versions and how to use a local SDK for private deployments.
[01:20] Liam O'Connor: For auth — our security team will want SSO and audit logs. How do you do enterprise auth?
[01:27] Evan Martinez: Good question. For hosted customers we support API keys plus SSO through SAML/Okta — the control plane supports SAML so you can provision teams. For Private we integrate with your KMS and HSM for key management. We'll share the SOC2 appendix.
[01:45] Ana Torres: Do you rotate keys automatically?
[01:47] Evan Martinez: We support key rotation APIs; for dedicated/private we recommend customer-managed KMS keys.
[01:54] Priya Desai: Back to the example — we show env var patterns. For local dev: REDWOOD_API_KEY in .env or use the SDK's credentials provider which reads from environment, from a credentials file, or from an instance metadata endpoint for dedicated infra.
[02:12] Marcus Lee: We run through a corporate proxy and our containers are locked down. Any tips?
[02:18] Priya Desai: We have a docs page for proxy settings — you can set REDWOOD_PROXY and the SDK will honor http(s)_proxy. For private deployments, traffic never traverses public endpoints if you run the control plane in your VPC.
[02:32] Sara Chen: Could you show the TypeScript example?
[02:34] Priya Desai: Yep. npm i @redwoodai/sdk, then import {Redwood} from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}); await client.generate({prompt: '...'}); We demo streaming using an event emitter and a callback.
[02:55] Evan Martinez: One piece we like to highlight: streaming reduces perceived latency and is simple in the TS SDK — you can start rendering tokens immediately.
[03:05] Priya Desai: I'll start a quick live run. Heads up the demo uses a small open model to keep latency quick.
[03:12] [03:12] Priya Desai: (typing) starting...
[03:18] [03:18] Priya Desai: Streaming chunks are coming in — you can see token deltas and partial text.
[03:25] Ana Torres: Looks smooth. How does batching work? We need to support many short queries per second.
[03:31] Priya Desai: Redwood runtime does continuous batching. In the SDK we provide opt-in batching settings: max_batch_size and max_wait_ms. You can tune by traffic shape; we can share recommendations based on your QPS.
[03:45] Marcus Lee: What about cost controls?
[03:47] Evan Martinez: You can set per-route settings in the console to cap token budgets, rate limits, and choose cheaper quantized models for certain routes. Optimize suggests quantization profiles too.
[03:58] Liam O'Connor: For the PoC we want to measure latency and token cost against our current provider. Can you export token-level logs?
[04:06] Priya Desai: Yes — Console has token-level traces, cost per request and detailed per-token breakdowns. We also provide a CSV export for benchmarks.
[04:15] Sara Chen: Any SDK examples for retries and idempotency? Sometimes our requests time out behind our proxy.
[04:21] Priya Desai: The SDK includes an auto-retry policy with exponential backoff and a request id header for idempotency. For long-running streams we recommend checkpointing with session IDs.
[04:35] Liam O'Connor: On private deployment — how long does a VPC/private install take?
[04:40] Evan Martinez: Typical Private installs are 4–6 weeks after network prep; Dedicated is faster for reserved capacity. For PoC we can do a hosted test in a day and then move to dedicated or private.
[04:55] Ana Torres: Our security team also wants to know about data retention and audit logs.
[05:00] Evan Martinez: By default, hosted logs are retained for 30 days, but enterprise customers can request extended retention. Audit logs include request metadata and user actions in the console. We'll send the security whitepaper.
[05:12] Marcus Lee: Is there TLS everywhere and mutual TLS option?
[05:15] Priya Desai: TLS is standard; mTLS can be configured for private endpoints.
[05:20] Sara Chen: Can you show the quickstart repo structure?
[05:22] Priya Desai: Sure. At the top level we have /python-quickstart and /ts-quickstart, example.env, Dockerfile, and a docker-compose for local testing. Also a benchmark script load_test.py that performs a series of short prompts and logs latency and token usage.
[05:38] [05:38] Priya Desai: (navigating) In python-quickstart main.py we call client.generate_stream and then print tokens as they arrive — the sample shows reconnect logic.
[05:48] Evan Martinez: Wanted to call out the SDK parity — both SDKs support streaming, function calling, structured output, and embeddings. We also have language bindings in Go and Java coming soon.
[06:01] Liam O'Connor: Any limits on model sizes? We have some longer contexts.
[06:05] Priya Desai: We support long context models up to 64k tokens depending on model choice; runtime selects best kernel and KV cache strategy. For heavy contexts we recommend dedicated capacity.
[06:18] Ana Torres: Cost/perf tradeoff — is there tooling to recommend quantization?
[06:22] Evan Martinez: Yes, Redwood Optimize analyzes your workload and recommends quantization profiles and batching parameters, with an estimated cost delta. We'll include a sample Optimize report.
[06:35] Sara Chen: For our PoC success metrics, we think: 95th p95 latency under 400ms for single-turn prompts, cost per 1K tokens under $X, and parity on output quality for our prompts. Is that realistic?
[06:48] Priya Desai: Sounds reasonable; we'll validate against your dataset. For p95 we often tune batch windows and dedicated capacity.
[06:55] Marcus Lee: If we hit a compliance blocker, can you do air-gapped installs?
[06:59] Evan Martinez: Yes, we have an on-prem package that can be deployed air-gapped; that's part of Private. It requires additional ops time.
[07:08] Liam O'Connor: Who should we expect to interact with during the PoC?
[07:11] Evan Martinez: Evan AE, Priya SE for integration and benchmarks, plus a solutions architect if the private install is required.
[07:18] Ana Torres: About rate limits and quotas, can we set per-team quotas in console?
[07:22] Priya Desai: Yes, console supports per-team routing and quotas, with overrides per route.
[07:27] Sara Chen: Do you have a sample docker image for offline testing?
[07:30] Priya Desai: We provide a dev image that simulates the runtime for basic testing; not for scale but useful for CI.
[07:36] Liam O'Connor: Ok, let's talk specifics — for the PoC we want a small dataset of 10k prompts, simulate 50 qps, and measure p95 and token cost. Is that doable in a hosted benchmark?
[07:46] Evan Martinez: Absolutely, we can spin up a benchmark run on hosted for a controlled window. Priya will coordinate the script we'll run.
[07:53] Priya Desai: I'll attach the load_test.py and a sample config. We'll need the dataset and ideal thresholds.
[07:59] Marcus Lee: Network: our egress must go through a proxy and we need IP allowlist — can you support static egress IPs?
[08:06] Evan Martinez: For dedicated we can provide static egress; for hosted we provide region endpoints and allowlist ranges. We'll send the allowlist ranges.
[08:17] Ana Torres: Any concerns on language model hallucination for our use case?
[08:20] Evan Martinez: We'll recommend guardrails: prompt engineering, reranking, and automated evals to detect regressions. Optimize ties into evals so you can get alerts for quality regression.
[08:33] Sara Chen: Regarding SDK telemetry — what metadata is collected by default?
[08:37] Priya Desai: Minimal telemetry: SDK version, request latency, error codes; no customer payload is sent. Payloads are never logged unless you enable debug and explicitly opt-in. We'll include the telemetry doc.
[08:50] Evan Martinez: Quick recap and next steps: we'll send the quickstart repo link, security docs, allowlist ranges, and propose PoC dates.
[08:59] Liam O'Connor: Sounds good.
[09:01] Ana Torres: Thanks everyone.
[09:03] Evan Martinez: Thanks — we'll follow up with the materials.
[09:06] [09:06] Call ends.

Note: timestamps after 09:06 are symbolic — the meeting ran approx 48 minutes; transcript above sampled key parts. Transcription contains a few misheard tokens (V PC vs VPC, kv cache as K V cache) and occasional speaker attribution errors which may be present in the original recording.
